'''Earl Christian Campbell''' (born March 29, 1955), nicknamed "'''the Tyler Rose'''", is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[running back]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for eight seasons, primarily with the [[Houston Oilers]]. Known for his aggressive, punishing running style, and ability to break tackles, Campbell gained recognition as one of the best power running backs in NFL history.

Campbell played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], where he won the [[Heisman Trophy]] and earned [[List of unanimous All-Americans in college football|unanimous All-American]] honors in his senior season, as well as numerous other accolades. Campbell was selected [[List of first overall National Football League Draft picks|first overall]] by the Oilers in the [[1978 NFL draft]], and had an immediate impact in the league, earning [[NFL Rookie of the Year]] honors. Campbell was also named the NFL's [[AP NFL Offensive Player of the Year Award|Offensive Player of the Year]] in each of his first three seasons, during which he averaged nearly 1,700 rushing yards per season. Campbell won the [[AP NFL Most Valuable Player Award]] in 1979 after leading the league in rushing yards and touchdowns.

With head coach [[Bum Phillips]], Campbell's emergence in Houston coincided with the [[Luv Ya Blue]] era, a period of sustained success in which the Oilers made three straight [[National Football League playoffs|playoff]] appearances. Campbell became the centerpiece of Houston's offense during the late 1970s and early 1980s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Aaseng |first=Nathan |date=2003 |title=African-American Athletes |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iSxylfm58foC&q=earl+campbell+oilers+offense&pg=PA42 |location=New York |publisher=Facts On File, Inc. |page=42 |isbn=0816048053 }}</ref> He was traded to the [[New Orleans Saints]] six games into the 1984 season, where he spent his final season and a half before retiring. Campbell was inducted into both the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] (1990) and [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] (1991). In 2019, he was named to the [[National Football League 100th Anniversary All-Time Team|NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]]. Campbell's jersey number is [[Retired number|retired]] by the University of Texas and the [[Tennessee Titans]].{{efn|name=fn1|The Oilers franchise moved to Tennessee in 1998 and was renamed the "Titans" in 1999.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tennessee Titans 2015 Media Guide - Historical Highlights|url=http://prod.static.titans.clubs.nfl.com/assets/docs/mediaguide/History_15_Historical_Highlights.pdf|website=titansonline.com|publisher=Tennessee Titans|access-date=July 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822153003/http://prod.static.titans.clubs.nfl.com/assets/docs/mediaguide/History_15_Historical_Highlights.pdf|archive-date=August 22, 2016}}</ref>}}

'''Dylan Colter Gandy''' (born March 8, 1982) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (American football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the fourth round of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Tech Red Raiders football|Texas Tech Red Raiders]].

Gandy won a Super Bowl with the Colts in [[Super Bowl XLI]] against the [[Chicago Bears]]. He was also a member of the [[Denver Broncos]], [[Oakland Raiders]], [[Detroit Lions]] and [[Chicago Bears]].

May 17, 1934 – April 25, 2014) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 21 seasons. He was the last remaining player from the 1950s still active in the NFL. He started for six teams, most notably the [[Baltimore Colts]] and [[Miami Dolphins]]. He became known as one of the greatest backup quarterbacks in NFL history, having served in the capacity for two Hall of Fame quarterbacks in [[Johnny Unitas]] and [[Bob Griese]]. An injury to Unitas in 1968 saw Morrall step in to become the starter; he guided the Colts to a 13–1 record and won league MVP. He also led them to their first [[1968 NFL Championship Game|NFL Championship]] win in nine years before ineffective play in [[Super Bowl III]] saw him benched for Unitas. Two years later, in [[Super Bowl V]], Morrall came off the bench for an injured Unitas and kept the Colts in the game before they ultimately won on a last-second field goal. In his first season with Miami in 1972, he came off the bench when Griese became injured early in the year, with Morrall winning all nine starts; Morrall started the first two playoff games, with Griese playing in each game before being named the starter for [[Super Bowl VII]], where the Dolphins completed [[1972 Miami Dolphins season|the only perfect season in NFL history]].

McCullouch''' (born January 10, 1946) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]] and was selected by the [[Detroit Lions]] in the first round of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft|1968 NFL draft]]. McCullouch was the world record holder for the 110 meter men's [[Hurdling|high hurdle sprint]] from July 1967 to July 1969. When attending the [[University of Southern California]], McCullouch was a member of the USC Track & Field teams (120 yard high hurdles and 4×110 sprint relay) in 1967 and 1968. The USC Track 4×110 yard relay team, for which McCullouch ran the start leg, set the world record in 1967 that remains today, as the metric 4 × 100 m relay is now the commonly contested event.

([[South Boston, Virginia]]) | college = [[East Tennessee State Buccaneers football|East Tennessee State]] | draftyear = 1982 | draftround = 5 | draftpick = 125 | pastteams = * [[Arizona Cardinals|St. Louis/Phoenix Cardinals]] ({{NFL Year|1982|1989}}) | statlabel1 = [[Carry (gridiron football)|Rushing yards]] | statvalue1 = 2,950 | statlabel2 = Average | statvalue2 = 4.3 | statlabel3 = Rushing [[touchdown]]s | statvalue3 = 24 | pfr = FerrEa00 }} '''Earl Thomas Ferrell''' (born March 27, 1958), is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[East Tennessee State Buccaneers football|East Tennessee State Buccaneers]] and was selected by the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] in the fifth round of the [[1982 NFL draft]]. Standing {{height|ft=6|in=0}} and 220 lbs., Ferrell played his entire NFL career for the Cardinals from 1982 to 1989. He led all Cardinals running backs in rushing yards during the 1988 and 1989 seasons, the team's first two years playing in [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]]. He was the second player, and one of only four in the school's history, to be selected in the draft and play in the NFL after playing [[college football]] at ETSU.[http://www.nfl.com/draft/history/fulldraft?abbr=E&collegeName=East+Tennessee+State&abbrFlag=0&type=school NFL Draft History Full Draft: East Tennessee State] After a [[Pro Bowl]] appearance in each of his final two seasons, Ferrell's career was cut short due to problems with illegal drugs. In 1988, Ferrell reportedly tested positive three times for [[cocaine]] and, before the 1990 season, he was suspended for one year because of another failed [[drug test]]. He never played in the NFL again.[https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C0CE0DC1531F935A15757C0A966958260 "Ferrell to Miss Season For Positive Drug Test"], ''New York Times'', April 26, 1990.
